lead: Every circuit is built from three passive elements: the resistor R, the inductor L and the capacitor C. Each element fixes one relation between its voltage v and its current i. That relation decides whether the element turns electrical energy into heat or stores it in a field. The same three laws let you read a phone charger, a motor drive or a filter on paper. This chapter gives the laws, their units, the power and energy behind them, and the ideal-versus-real gap you must watch in exams.

sections.h3: Voltage, current and the three element laws

blocks.text: Voltage v is the energy per charge across an element, measured in volts (V). Current i is the charge flow through it, measured in amperes (A). Use the passive sign convention: current enters the positive voltage terminal. A passive element has no internal source.

A resistor obeys v = iR. R is resistance in ohms (Ω); 1 Ω = 1 V/A. An inductor obeys v = L di/dt. L is inductance in henries (H); 1 H = 1 V·s/A. A capacitor obeys i = C dv/dt. C is capacitance in farads (F); 1 F = 1 A·s/V. The derivative means the element reacts to change, not to the present value alone.
v_R = iR,  v_L = L di/dt,  i_C = C dv/dt
blocks.where: v_R is resistor voltage in V; i is current in A; R is resistance in Ω; v_L is inductor voltage in V; L is inductance in H; t is time in s; i_C is capacitor current in A; C is capacitance in F; v is capacitor voltage in V.

blocks.text: For a resistor, the V-I characteristic is a straight line through the origin; some syllabi call it the volt-ampere characteristic. All three elements are linear when R, L and C are constant, passive because they cannot supply net energy, and bilateral because reversing the terminals does not change the law. Ohm's law gets its full treatment in 1.3.

sections.h3: Power and energy: dissipate or store

blocks.text: Power p = vi is the rate of energy flow, measured in watts (W). For a resistor, p = vi = i²R = v²/R. This power is never negative, so a resistor turns electrical energy into heat. A filament lamp and a heater are resistors doing useful work.

For an inductor, p = vi = L i di/dt = d/dt(½Li²). The stored magnetic energy is W_L = ½Li² joules (J). For a capacitor, p = vi = C v dv/dt = d/dt(½Cv²). The stored electric energy is W_C = ½Cv² J. Ideal L and C store energy and return it later; they do not dissipate it.

Real elements are not perfect. A real inductor has winding resistance, so model it as an ideal L in series with a small resistance. That resistance dissipates i²R_w and limits the quality of filters and transformers. A real capacitor has leakage and equivalent series resistance, but the ideal law still sets the main behaviour.

items: Name the element and the known variable: voltage v or current i.
Write the matching law: v = iR for R, v = L di/dt for L, i = C dv/dt for C.
Convert prefixes before calculating: 100 μF = 100 × 10⁻⁶ F, 50 mH = 50 × 10⁻³ H.
Check units: H × A/s gives V; F × V/s gives A; V × A gives W.

blocks.text: At DC steady state, di/dt = 0 makes an ideal inductor a short circuit (v = 0). dv/dt = 0 makes an ideal capacitor an open circuit (i = 0). A resistor still obeys v = iR at DC. Do not use v = iR for L or C; their laws are differential. For a sinusoidal signal, the derivative also brings a 90° phase shift; phasors in Unit 3 turn that calculus into algebra. Time-domain transients and time constants are in Unit 5, Transient Analysis and Laplace Transform.
Series and parallel combinations, and voltage and current division, come in 1.5. For now, treat each element alone and trust its law.

examples.question: A 12 Ω resistor carries 2 A. A 0.5 H inductor carries 2 A and has di/dt = 40 A/s. A 100 μF capacitor has 10 V across it and dv/dt = 200 V/s. Find the resistor voltage v_R, the inductor voltage v_L, the capacitor current i_C, and the energy stored in the inductor and capacitor.
steps: Resistor law: v_R = iR = 2 A × 12 Ω = 24 V.
Inductor law: v_L = L di/dt = 0.5 H × 40 A/s = 20 V.
Capacitor law: i_C = C dv/dt = 100 × 10⁻⁶ F × 200 V/s = 0.02 A = 20 mA.
Inductor stored energy: W_L = ½Li² = ½ × 0.5 H × (2 A)² = 1 J.
Capacitor stored energy: W_C = ½Cv² = ½ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ F × (10 V)² = 0.005 J = 5 mJ.

dvdt = 200.0

traps: Using v = iR for an inductor or capacitor. Their laws are v = L di/dt and i = C dv/dt.
Swapping the two differential laws: inductor voltage uses di/dt; capacitor current uses dv/dt.
Forgetting prefix powers: 100 μF is 100 × 10⁻⁶ F, not 100 × 10⁻³ F.
Treating ideal L and C as energy dissipaters. They store and return energy; R dissipates it.
Ignoring the winding resistance of a real inductor, which adds a resistive voltage drop.

quiz.q: Define resistance R, inductance L and capacitance C. Give the unit of each.
quiz.a: R is resistance in ohms (Ω). L is inductance in henries (H). C is capacitance in farads (F).

quiz.q: Why is an ideal inductor a short circuit at DC steady state?
quiz.a: At DC steady state, di/dt = 0, so v_L = L di/dt = 0. A zero-voltage element is a short circuit.

quiz.q: A 2 kΩ resistor carries 5 mA. Find its voltage and power.
A 0.2 H inductor has current rising at 100 A/s. Find v_L.
quiz.a: v_L = L di/dt = 0.2 H × 100 A/s = 20 V.

quiz.q: A 100 μF capacitor has v = 10 V and dv/dt = -50 V/s. Find i_C and state the current direction.
quiz.a: i_C = C dv/dt = 100 × 10⁻⁶ F × (-50 V/s) = -0.005 A = -5 mA. The negative sign means current flows opposite the chosen positive terminal direction.

quiz.q: Which passive element dissipates energy, and which elements store it?
quiz.a: The resistor dissipates energy as heat. The ideal inductor stores magnetic energy ½Li². The ideal capacitor stores electric energy ½Cv².

quiz.q: A real inductor has 0.4 H and winding resistance 5 Ω. It carries 2 A DC. Find the terminal voltage at steady state.
quiz.a: At DC, di/dt = 0, so the ideal L part has 0 V. The winding resistance drops iR_w = 2 A × 5 Ω = 10 V. The terminal voltage is 10 V.

beyond: Not for the exam. In power electronics, the same laws size inductors in a buck converter and capacitors in a laptop charger. IC designers treat parasitic L and C as circuit elements at gigahertz frequencies. Search next for inductor saturation, capacitor ESR, and parasitic extraction.
